pos: n. (the Scottish border county named for a royal burgh that was fought over until it disappeared, leaving only earthworks)
etymology: Old English Hrocesburh, Hroc's fort; the burgh stood between the Tweed and the Teviot.
biblical_def: Roxburgh is the Scottish border county of Teviotdale and Liddesdale, and it is named after a town that no longer exists. Roxburgh was one of the four great royal burghs of twelfth-century Scotland, with a mint, a castle and a sheriff, standing on the tongue of land where the Teviot runs into the Tweed; Alexander II was married there and Alexander III born there. Because it lay on the frontier it changed hands repeatedly through the wars of independence and after, was held by the English for long periods, and was besieged again and again; James II was killed by the bursting of one of his own guns while besieging it in 1460. After its final capture the Scots levelled the castle, and the burgh never recovered. Nothing is left but grassed earthworks in a field and a village a mile away that carries the name. The county afterwards held the abbeys of Kelso and Jedburgh and, in the seventeenth century, a stubborn covenanting population in the upland parishes. The dictionary enters the vanished burgh as a text on the permanence of cities, which Scripture treats as a settled question.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a burgh as a corporate town; a rampart as an elevation of earth round a place; to raze as to level with the ground; continuing as lasting; and a foundation as the basis of a building.
webster_full: BURGH, n. A borough; a corporate town; a town that sends representatives to parliament.
RAMPART, n. An elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
RAZE, v.t. To subvert from the foundation; to overthrow; to destroy; to level with the ground.
CONTINUING, ppr. Remaining fixed or permanent; lasting; enduring; persevering.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that upon which anything stands and is supported.
scriptures: For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Lam 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Amo 6:1
Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!
corruption_summary: Scottish border county named for a royal burgh with a mint and a castle that was besieged until it was levelled after 1460, leaving only grassed earthworks in a field.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no city is permanent and that Christians are not supposed to be surprised by this. Roxburgh had a mint, a castle, a sheriff and royal births, and it is now a shape in the grass. The writer to the Hebrews states the believer's position in one sentence that settles the whole question of civic attachment: “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). That is not a counsel of indifference to the places men live in, since Scripture also commands prayer and labour for a city's peace; it is a refusal to found hope on masonry.

The second thing to recover is the proper reading of such a ruin, which is neither romantic nor fatalistic. Lamentations describes a city taken and does not soften it, recording that “Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars” (Lam 2:9), and attributing the act to God rather than to circumstance. The risen Christ warns a church that a candlestick may be removed from its place, bidding it “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5). And Amos names the state of mind in which such losses are not expected, pronouncing woe on those “that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations” (Amo 6:1). A county that bears the name of a town nobody can find is a cheap lesson in a subject usually taught expensively.

pos: n. (the Border burgh of the souters whose contingent was destroyed at Flodden in 1513 and which keeps the casting of the colours for them)
etymology: Old English sele cirice, the hall church or the church by the dwelling; the burgh stands above the Ettrick in the Border forest.
biblical_def: Selkirk is the Border burgh standing above the Ettrick Water in what was the royal forest, and its people were called souters from the shoemaking that was their trade. David I planted a Tironensian abbey there in 1113, though it was moved to Kelso fifteen years later. The town's memory is fixed on one day. At Flodden, on the ninth of September 1513, James IV took an army into England and lost it; the king, nine earls, fourteen lords, an archbishop, two bishops and some ten thousand men were killed in an afternoon, and the small burghs of the Borders and the Lothians were stripped of a generation. Tradition holds that eighty men went from Selkirk and one returned, Fletcher, carrying a captured English standard, and that he cast it down in the market place without words because he could not say what had happened. The burgh still casts the colours each June in the Common Riding. The dictionary records Flodden as a national bereavement and sets against the romance of it the plain biblical account of what a king's vanity costs a people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lamentation as the expression of sorrow; bereaved as deprived of friends by death; a standard as an ensign or flag; to comfort as to console; and a souter as a shoemaker.
webster_full: LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
BEREAVED, pp. Deprived; stripped and left destitute; deprived of friends or relations by death.
STANDARD, n. An ensign of war; a staff with a flag or colours; a banner borne by an army.
COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen; to invigorate; to console; to cheer the mind under affliction.
SOUTER, n. A shoemaker; a cobbler; a term still used in Scotland.
scriptures: Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.
Mat 2:18
In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
corruption_summary: Border burgh of the souters whose contingent was destroyed at Flodden on 9 September 1513, where James IV, nine earls, two bishops and some ten thousand men were killed in an afternoon.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the chivalric vanity that produced Flodden, and the dictionary names it as sin rather than misfortune. James IV had no necessity upon him. He invaded England in fulfilment of an alliance with France, having been warned, and he fought the battle on foot in the front rank where a king can neither see nor command, because that was the gallant thing to do; the result was that the whole command structure of the kingdom died together on one slope. Scripture does not supply romance for such an event. Jeremiah gives the sound of it: “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not” (Jer 31:15). Matthew repeats it over another massacre of a town's sons, that “In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning” (Mat 2:18).

The second paragraph is for the mourners rather than the king, because the eighty that went from one small burgh had no part in the decision. The psalm gives the church language for being destroyed in a cause it did not choose, “for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22), and that language is not despair but address: it is spoken to God, which is the whole difference between lament and complaint. Micah supplies the one thing a stripped town may say to those who are glad of it: “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me” (Mic 7:8). The dictionary records that Selkirk's way of remembering, a man casting a flag down in silence because there is nothing to report, is better theology than most war memorials manage.

“we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22) — a cause the souters did not choose.

pos: n. (the Tweeddale burgh whose Cross Kirk was built over a supposed fragment of the true cross found in 1261 and became a royal pilgrimage)
etymology: Brittonic pebyll, tents or shielings, the plural giving the burgh its name; the town stands on the Tweed.
biblical_def: Peebles is the burgh on the upper Tweed, the county town of Peeblesshire, and its medieval importance rested on a relic. In 1261, so the chroniclers report, workmen digging on the site of an old church found a stone cross and, soon after, a quantity of bones and an inscription taken to refer to one of the companions of a third-century martyr; the cross was declared a fragment of the true cross. Alexander III founded the Cross Kirk over the spot, a Trinitarian friary was attached to serve it, and the shrine became a pilgrimage that drew Scottish kings, James II, James III and James IV among them, with the Beltane fair and a steady traffic in offerings. The relic was lost at the Reformation and the friary suppressed; the Cross Kirk served as the parish church until 1784 and is now a roofless shell. The dictionary enters Peebles as the clearest Scottish instance of a devotion manufactured out of an archaeological accident, and names the general rule rather than disputing the find, since the rule disposes of the matter whatever was in the ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint preserved with veneration; a shrine as a case for sacred things; an offering as that presented in worship; to flee as to run from; and unclean as foul or polluted.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; the body of a deceased person, or some part of it, preserved with veneration.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; the tomb of a saint, resorted to by devotees.
OFFERING, n. That which is presented in divine worship or service; a sacrifice; an oblation.
FLEE, v.i. To run with rapidity, as from danger; to attempt to escape; to hasten from.
UNCLEAN, a. Foul; dirty; filthy; in the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; morally impure.
scriptures: Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Jer 10:5
They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
corruption_summary: Tweeddale burgh whose Cross Kirk was founded by Alexander III over a cross and bones dug up in 1261 and declared a fragment of the true cross, drawing royal pilgrimages until the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the cult of the true cross, and the dictionary names it without needing to adjudicate what the workmen of 1261 actually found. The point is prior to the archaeology. Even on the most favourable supposition, a piece of the wood on which Christ died is a piece of wood; it has no virtue, confers no merit, hears no prayer and performs no cure, and a religion organised around it is a religion directed to an object. The commandment covers the making and the use together: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Paul's word to a church surrounded by shrines is a single imperative, “flee from idolatry” (1Co 10:14), and it does not pause to examine credentials.

The second paragraph names the comfort in the matter, because Scripture handles idols with mockery as well as prohibition. Jeremiah describes the manufactured object as helpless in both directions, unable to speak, unable to walk, carried about by its own devotees, and then draws the conclusion that it cannot hurt anybody either: “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5). A burgh that built a friary, a fair and a royal pilgrimage over a hole in the ground was not in the grip of a power; it was in the grip of a mistake, and when the relic went the town carried on. The duty of those who see it is to leave, and the command is express: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing” (2Co 6:17). The Cross Kirk stood as the parish church of Peebles for two centuries after its relic was gone, which the dictionary counts the best use it was ever put to.

“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — the duty of those who see it.

pos: n. (the Scottish border county of the Merse, birthplace of Duns Scotus, whose name became the English word dunce)
etymology: From Berwick, Old English bere wic, the barley farm; the county retains the name though the town of Berwick passed to England in 1482.
biblical_def: Berwickshire is the Scottish border county of the fertile plain called the Merse, running from the Lammermuirs down to the Tweed, and it keeps the name of a town that has been English since 1482. Its village of Duns gave the medieval church one of its greatest intellects. John Duns Scotus, born there about 1266, became the Subtle Doctor, a Franciscan who taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne, defended the immaculate conception of the Virgin, argued the primacy of the will over the intellect, and built an apparatus of formal distinctions so fine that his successors could not agree what he had meant. When the humanists and then the Reformers turned on the schoolmen, Scotus became the type of the subtlety that proves nothing, and his followers were called Dunses; from that the English word dunce descends, which is the most ironic fate in the history of learning. In 1639 the covenanting army mustered on Duns Law in the same parish, and the county was afterward solidly Presbyterian. The dictionary records both facts about Duns, and holds that the disgrace of a great mind is a warning about method rather than about ability.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a schoolman as one versed in the niceties of the schools; subtlety as refinement or nicety of distinction; a dunce as a dullard; doctrine as that which is taught; and reading as the public perusal of Scripture.
webster_full: SCHOOLMAN, n. A man versed in the niceties of academical disputation, or of school divinity.
SUBTLETY, n. Thinness; fineness; refinement; extreme acuteness; cunning; artifice.
DUNCE, n. A person of weak intellect; a dullard; one who is incapable of learning.
DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principle or position in any science; whatever is laid down as true.
READING, n. The act of perusing; a public lecture or recitation; the study of books.
scriptures: For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Scottish border county of the Merse whose village of Duns produced John Duns Scotus about 1266 and whose name became the English word dunce, and where the covenanting army mustered on Duns Law in 1639.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is scholastic method as it had become by the fourteenth century, and the dictionary is careful about the charge. The objection is not to distinctions, nor to logic, nor to the use of reason in divinity; Reformed orthodoxy made heavy use of all three and the Reformers were trained schoolmen themselves. The objection is to a method that spun distinctions out of distinctions without a controlling text, so that a question was settled by whoever could draw the finer line, and the whole of it rested on authorities and traditions the Scriptures had never established. Paul warns that God deliberately chose a method that would look foolish to such men, since “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).

The second paragraph names the test that was missing and the irony that followed. Isaiah supplies the control: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Where that control is absent, apparatus multiplies and settles nothing, and Paul describes the result as impressive and empty, having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23). The remedy he prescribes to a young minister is almost crude by comparison and is in three words: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). Scotus was not a dunce; he was one of the ablest men of his age, and his name became a byword for stupidity because he spent that ability on a method that could not be checked. The dictionary enters the fact as the sharpest available warning to clever men in theology, and notes that three and a half centuries later the ploughmen of the same parish were mustering on Duns Law for a confession they could state in a page.

roots_lines: Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness, absurdity; “by the foolishness of preaching”, 1 Corinthians 1:21.

pos: n. (the Border abbey of the Cistercians, burned repeatedly in the wars and surrendered at the Reformation, where Bruce's heart is said to lie)
etymology: Brittonic mailros, the bare moor or bare promontory, from mail, bare, and ros, a moor; the original site was at Old Melrose.
biblical_def: Melrose is the Border town on the Tweed under the Eildon hills, and its abbey was the first Cistercian house in Scotland, founded by David I in 1136 with monks from Rievaulx. It was rich, holding great sheep runs across the Border hills, and it was ruined by its position: burned by Edward II in 1322, burned again by Richard II in 1385, and wrecked by Hertford's army in 1545 in the campaign called the Rough Wooing. The abbey was never properly rebuilt and the last monk died in 1590. A lead casket containing a heart was found beneath the chapter house floor in 1921 and again in 1996, and is taken to be the heart of Robert the Bruce, which he directed should be carried to the Holy Land and was brought back. The parish worshipped in the nave after the Reformation. The dictionary records the house for what its ruin teaches about the wealth of monasteries, and names the burial of a king's heart as a piece of the same religion as the relics: an attempt to purchase by arrangement what cannot be arranged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a monastery as a house of religious retirement; a chapter house as the building where a convent meets; cieled as panelled; a sepulchre as a tomb; and to deface as to disfigure.
webster_full: MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from the world, for persons devoted to religion.
CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the monks of a convent, or of the clergy of a cathedral; the place of such assembly.
CIELED, pp. Covered or overlaid with boards or plaster; furnished with a ceiling.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
DEFACE, v.t. To destroy or mar the face or surface of a thing; to disfigure; to injure the beauty of.
scriptures: Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: First Cistercian house in Scotland, founded in 1136 and holding great Border sheep runs, burned in 1322, 1385 and 1545, where a lead casket taken for Bruce's heart was found beneath the chapter house.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the accumulation itself, and the dictionary names it as the monastic system's own undoing rather than merely as an abuse within it. Melrose was founded by men vowed to poverty and became one of the great wool producers of northern Britain, with granges, flocks, tithes and courts; the wealth drew armies, and three burnings in two centuries were the price. Haggai's question about priorities is the right one to ask of a house that was magnificent while its tenants' parishes went unpreached: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The psalmist's lament over a sanctuary handled roughly applies to the burnings without excusing what was burnt, for “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7).

The second paragraph names the heart under the chapter house floor, because that is where this entry earns its place. Bruce directed that his heart be carried on crusade to the Holy Land, and when it came back it was buried in the richest abbey in his gift. Both halves of that arrangement are the same religion: a work performed by proxy, in a place reckoned holy, to secure something at the end for a man who could not do it himself. The Lord's word about religion that is splendid outside and dead within is the word for a gilded casket in a consecrated floor: “ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones” (Mat 23:27). What the Scriptures hold out instead is not a better tomb but a different city, since “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). The dictionary notes that Melrose's most useful period began when the parish started worshipping in the nave of the ruin.

pos: n. (the Border abbey of the Tironensians, greatest of the four, whose surviving transept served as the parish kirk until 1771)
etymology: Old English calc hoh, the chalk or limestone heugh, the spur of rock above the Tweed where the abbey stands.
biblical_def: Kelso is the Border town where the Teviot joins the Tweed, and its abbey was the greatest of the four great houses of the Scottish Borders. The Tironensian community that David I had planted at Selkirk in 1113 was moved there in 1128, and the church they built, with a double transept and a massive west tower, was the largest and richest in the region; the abbot had precedence over all other Scottish abbots and the house held some forty churches. James III was crowned in it in 1460 as a boy of eight. Like Melrose it was destroyed by war rather than by reformers, burned in 1523 and again in 1542, and finally stormed by Hertford's force in 1545, when the defenders, including twelve monks, were killed in the tower. After the Reformation the parish fitted up the surviving western transept as its kirk, built a floor and galleries inside it and worshipped there for two centuries until the structure was condemned in 1771. The dictionary records the transept kirk with approval and states the principle it illustrates.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a transept as the cross aisle of a church; a gallery as a raised floor for spectators; to fit up as to prepare for use; a plummet as a weight for sounding; and small things as matters of little account.
webster_full: TRANSEPT, n. In architecture, the cross aisle of a church, lying across the nave at right angles.
GALLERY, n. A covered passage; in a church, an elevated floor or platform for the accommodation of hearers.
FIT, v.t. To adapt; to suit; to make suitable; to prepare; to furnish with what is proper.
PLUMMET, n. A long piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water; a plumb line.
SMALL, a. Slender; thin; fine; of little size; minute; of little consequence or importance.

But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy:
Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Hab 2:20
But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.
corruption_summary: Greatest of the four Border abbeys, Tironensian from 1128, where James III was crowned in 1460 and whose defenders were killed in the tower in 1545, its surviving transept serving as the parish kirk until 1771.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a building exists for the congregation that uses it, and that fitting a floor and galleries into the stump of a ruined abbey is a better act than either venerating the ruin or pulling it down for stone. Kelso's parish did the sensible thing for two hundred years. Ezra records the mixed feeling that attends such work honestly, for when the foundation of the second house was laid the old men who had seen the first “wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12); both reactions were right, and neither stopped the building.

The second thing to recover is Zechariah's rebuke to those who measure a work by its grandeur, which was spoken to men rebuilding a temple that would not match what had stood there: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). A parish in a transept is a day of small things, and so is almost every genuine recovery. Nehemiah's way of putting the proposal is the pattern for it, a statement of the facts followed immediately by a call to work: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). What the finished thing is for is stated by Habakkuk, and it is not architecture: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). The dictionary notes that the abbot of Kelso once took precedence over every abbot in Scotland, and that the most useful thing the house ever did was to leave a transept big enough to hold a parish.

pos: n. (the Border abbey town whose summary Border courts gave Scots the phrase Jethart justice, hanging first and trying afterwards)
etymology: Old English Gedwearde, the enclosure on the Jed water; the Scots form is Jethart.
biblical_def: Jedburgh is the Roxburghshire town on the Jed water, eight miles from the English line, and it holds the Augustinian abbey David I founded about 1138, whose roofless nave still stands nearly complete. The town's castle was demolished by the Scots themselves in 1409 to stop the English using it, and a gaol was later built on the site. Because Jedburgh was the seat of the justiciar's court for the middle march, it became the place where the Border was governed, which meant the suppression of the reiving families by whatever means the warden had; the phrase Jethart justice, meaning to hang a man first and try him after, records what that government looked like from below, and is traditionally attached to the circuit of 1510 or to Lord Home's expedition. Mary Queen of Scots held a justice ayre there in 1566 and nearly died of a fever in the house still shown. The dictionary enters the phrase because it is a proverb about law, and because the distinction between the magistrate's lawful sword and the summary convenience of a strong man is one Scripture draws sharply.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines summary as done without the usual forms of law; a justiciar as a chief justice; to hang as to suspend by the neck; a sword as a weapon of offence; and a minister as an agent or servant.
webster_full: SUMMARY, a. Reduced into a narrow compass; short; done without the usual forms and delays of law.
JUSTICIARY, n. An administrator of justice; a chief justice, as in the ancient courts of Scotland.
HANG, v.t. To suspend; to put to death by suspending by the neck.
SWORD, n. An offensive weapon worn at the side; the emblem of judicial vengeance or of war.
MINISTER, n. An agent; one who acts under the authority of another; a servant; a magistrate.
scriptures: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Border abbey town and seat of the justiciar's court for the middle march, whose summary suppression of the reiving families gave Scots the phrase Jethart justice, hanging first and trying afterwards.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is summary justice, and the dictionary names it as a corruption of an office that it otherwise defends. The Border was genuinely lawless and the reiving families genuinely murderous; the wardens were given an impossible task and the men they hanged were mostly guilty of something. None of that makes a hanging without trial a judgment. Scripture grants the magistrate a real sword for a defined purpose, and the grant carries the restriction inside it: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). A minister acts under instruction, and an officer who dispenses with the finding of fact has stopped ministering and started deciding.

The second paragraph names the mechanism, because the Border courts were not mobs. They were courts, sitting under authority, with records; they simply arranged the order so that the sentence preceded the proof. That is the exact thing the psalmist calls iniquity enthroned: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20). What the people under such a government feel is noted by Solomon as a reliable index of its character, since “when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2), and a proverb coined by the governed is a verdict of that kind. The requirement on any man holding such power is stated once and briefly and leaves no room for Jethart justice: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The dictionary observes that the phrase has outlasted every warden who earned it.

Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; “which frameth mischief by a law”, Psalm 94:20.

pos: n. (the Teviotdale town of the Border reivers and later of the hosiery trade, whose upland parishes were left without preaching for generations)
etymology: Old English haga wic, the hedged or enclosed dwelling, from haga, a hedge or enclosure, and wic, a settlement.
biblical_def: Hawick is the largest town of Teviotdale, standing where the Slitrig joins the Teviot in the heart of what was the middle march. Through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries this was reiving country: the Armstrongs, Elliots, Scotts and Douglases on the Scottish side and the Charltons and Robsons on the English raided one another's cattle, took blackmail, burned farms and killed, and the warden system contained them only intermittently; Hawick itself was burned by the English in 1570. The country was poor, the parishes were enormous and the stipends tiny, and the consequence was a long want of ministers in the upland parishes. After the union of the crowns in 1603 the Borders were pacified with great severity, and in the eighteenth century Hawick turned to stocking-making and became a hosiery town. The dictionary enters Hawick to put the two things side by side, a violent district and an unserved one, and to name which of the two the church was answerable for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blackmail as a tribute formerly paid for protection; a reiver's root, to reave, as to plunder; a hedge as a fence of shrubs; a gap as a breach; and a stipend as settled pay.
webster_full: BLACKMAIL, n. A certain rate of money, corn, cattle or other thing, anciently paid in the north of England and in Scotland to persons allied with robbers, to be protected from pillage.
REAVE, v.t. To take away by violence; to bereave; to rob or plunder.
HEDGE, n. A fence or boundary formed of thorn bushes or other shrubs planted close together.
GAP, n. An opening; a breach; a passage made by breaking or parting; a hiatus.
STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
scriptures: And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
corruption_summary: Teviotdale town in the heart of the middle march, burned by the English in 1570, whose reiving families were pacified only after 1603 and whose upland parishes went for generations without a preaching ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is a failure of our own, and the dictionary insists on the order in which the two charges fall. The reivers were violent men and their blackmail, cattle-lifting and killing need no defence; but the church had held the Borders for four centuries before the Reformation and two after it, and left whole upland parishes with no preaching, no catechising and a stipend no educated man would take. Ezekiel's indictment is about an absence rather than a crime, and it falls on the watchmen: “And I sought for a man among them, that should make up the hedge, and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I should not destroy it: but I found none” (Eze 22:30). A district cannot be reformed by wardens if it has never been taught.

The second paragraph asks the psalmist's question and answers it as Scripture answers it, which is not with a scheme of pacification. “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) is the question of a man in exactly Teviotdale's position, and the psalm's reply is that the LORD is in his holy temple and sees. What is given to the few in such a country is a particular courage, since “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1), and the reiving families, for all their horses, were the ones who had to keep watch at night. What is required of them is not withdrawal to a better district but intercession and labour in the one they have: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7). The Borders were eventually quieted by hangings and transportations after 1603, and the dictionary records that this was the state's remedy and not the church's, and that the church had not tried its own.

pos: n. (the Nithsdale burgh at whose cross Richard Cameron and twenty men posted the declaration disowning Charles II on 22 June 1680)
etymology: Gaelic sean cathair, the old fort, from sean, old, and cathair, a fort or stronghold.
biblical_def: Sanquhar is the small burgh of upper Nithsdale in Dumfriesshire, on the road between Ayrshire and Dumfries, with a castle of the Crichtons above it and the oldest working post office in Britain. Its day is the twenty-second of June 1680. Richard Cameron, a field preacher who had been ordained in Holland, rode into the burgh with his brother Michael, Michael Cargill and about twenty armed men, drew up at the market cross, sang a psalm, prayed, and read and affixed a declaration which disowned Charles Stuart as king on the ground that he had broken his covenant engagements, usurped the headship of Christ's church and shed the blood of the saints, and declared war against him and all who adhered to him. A reward was set on Cameron's head; he was killed at Airds Moss on the twenty-second of July, a month later, and his head and hands were carried to Edinburgh. Cargill excommunicated the king at Torwood in September and was executed the following year. The dictionary records the declaration, states the one point in it that is certainly true, and names the one that is not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a declaration as a public avowal; to disown as to refuse to acknowledge; a usurper as one who seizes power without right; allegiance as the obligation of a subject; and supremacy as the state of being highest in authority.
webster_full: DECLARATION, n. An affirmation; a public avowal or proclamation; a publishing or making known.
DISOWN, v.t. To deny; not to own; to refuse to acknowledge as belonging to one's self.
USURPER, n. One who seizes or occupies the power or property of another without right.
ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; loyalty.
SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: Nithsdale burgh at whose market cross Richard Cameron and about twenty men read and affixed a declaration disowning Charles II on 22 June 1680, a month before Cameron was killed at Airds Moss.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary states first the point the Sanquhar men had right, because it is the point the whole quarrel turned on. Charles II had taken to himself a supremacy over the church of Christ, imposing ministers, forbidding assemblies, and requiring oaths acknowledging his headship; that claim is false, and no subject owes obedience to it. The apostolic answer to a magistrate commanding in the things of God is not negotiable: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The three in Babylon give the form of the refusal, telling a king to his face “that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18), and offering nothing further.

The corruption to name is the step beyond that, and the dictionary names it against men it honours. The Sanquhar Declaration did not merely refuse an unlawful command; it disowned the king's civil authority altogether and declared war. That is a different act, and Scripture does not authorise it. Paul wrote under Nero, whose claims and cruelties exceeded anything the Stuarts attempted, and he wrote “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1). Solomon forbids the political combination by its plainest name, “fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21). Twenty men at a market cross declaring war on a kingdom achieved the death of Cameron within a month, of Cargill within a year, and of Renwick in 1688, and furnished the government with the pretext for the Killing Times. The dictionary holds that refusal unto blood was the course, and that the sword at the cross was a sin which the courage of the men who drew it does not convert into a virtue.

roots_lines: Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, power, jurisdiction; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to subject, to put in subjection; “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers”, Romans 13:1.
Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; “We ought to obey God rather than men”, Acts 5:29.

“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero.

pos: n. (the Galloway burgh where Margaret Wilson and Margaret McLachlan were drowned at stakes in the Bladnoch in May 1685 for refusing the Abjuration oath)
etymology: Old English or Norse wic tun, the settlement by the bay or creek, from wic, a bay or dwelling, and tun, a town.
biblical_def: Wigtown is the old county town of Wigtownshire in Galloway, standing above the tidal flats where the Bladnoch runs into the bay. In May 1685, in the last months of the persecution, two women were executed there by drowning. Margaret McLachlan, a widow of about sixty-three from Kirkinner, and Margaret Wilson, a farmer's daughter of eighteen from Glenvernoch, had refused the Abjuration oath, which required the swearer to renounce the Sanquhar Declaration and acknowledge the king's supremacy; they were condemned and tied to stakes driven into the sand so that the rising tide would take them. The older woman was placed further out so that the younger might see her die and be moved to swear; she did not. Wigtown kirkyard holds their graves and the burgh a monument. The dictionary records the case as the sharpest instance in British history of an oath used as an instrument of execution, and it refuses the argument, still occasionally made, that the sentence was commuted and the drownings never happened.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to abjure as to renounce upon oath; an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God; to drown as to deprive of life by immersion; constancy as firmness of mind; and to overcome as to conquer.
webster_full: ABJURE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon; to retract or recant a declaration upon oath.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to deprive of life by immersion in water or other fluid.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in attachments or in principle.
OVERCOME, v.t. To conquer; to vanquish; to subdue; to surmount; to get the better of.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Isa 43:2

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
corruption_summary: Galloway burgh where Margaret McLachlan, about sixty-three, and Margaret Wilson, eighteen, were tied to stakes in the Bladnoch in May 1685 and drowned by the rising tide for refusing the Abjuration oath.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the test oath, and Wigtown is where its nature is clearest. The Abjuration oath did not ask a woman to commit a crime or to deny the faith in words; it asked her to renounce a declaration and to acknowledge a supremacy, and the government made swearing it the condition of life. That is the use of conscience as the executioner's instrument, and it is worse rather than better than a simple sentence, because it requires the victim's own hand in her death. The arithmetic our Lord supplies is what two women on a sandbank had to work with: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28). The older woman was staked further out so that the girl would watch, which is the refinement that tells one everything about the policy.

The second paragraph names a corruption of the record, because it is still at work. Through the nineteenth century and since, it has been argued that the sentence was reprieved, that the drownings are a legend, and that the Wigtown story is Covenanting propaganda. The dictionary rejects the argument: the sentence, the refusal, the local testimony and the kirk-session record stand, and the chief ground for doubt has always been that the thing is too dreadful to have been done by a government. It was done. The promise the two women had is not a promise of rescue, since they were not rescued: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee” (Isa 43:2), which means what the martyrs took it to mean and not what a comfortable reader wants it to mean. Their condition is the church's ordinary condition, “for thy sake are we killed all the day long” (Psa 44:22), and their victory is located outside themselves: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).
